name: Sucrose (sugar) solution by mouth
short: Newborns with undiagnosed hereditary fructose intolerance: liver failure from formulas with fructose (4 cases). Preterm, >10 doses a day in week 1: poorer neurodevelopment (1 trial). Gel: no data.
text: Form covered: sucrose solution given by mouth to infants only; this entry does not cover sucrose gel put in the vagina. Inherited fructose intolerance (case reports; formulas, not sucrose solution): four newborns with undiagnosed hereditary fructose intolerance developed life-threatening acute liver failure from fructose-containing infant formulas; the authors note that some formulas contain fructose as sucrose, which is made of fructose and glucose, and the abstract does not say which form each formula contained. No adverse-event results were found for sucrose gel put in the vagina: two gel trial abstracts state that safety was assessed or side effects recorded but give no results, and the abstract of a 560-woman gel trial does not mention safety. Infants with colic: the colic trial abstracts cited on the colic page do not report adverse events, and a Cochrane review of pain-relieving agents for colic reports no serious adverse events for any agent except dicyclomine (a drug). In a double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 83 infants aged 1 to 3 months given sucrose solution or placebo by mouth before bladder catheterisation (a different use), no adverse events were reported. Newborns given sucrose for painful procedures (a different use): a Cochrane review of 74 trials (7049 infants) found that reported adverse effects were minor and similar in the sucrose and control groups and that no serious side effects or harms have been documented, while the effects on long-term development are unknown; a later Cochrane review of heel-lance trials reports that minor adverse events required no intervention; and in a dose-finding trial in 245 neonates born at 24 to 42 weeks, 5 (2.0%) had adverse events, all of which resolved without medical intervention. Repeated doses: a systematic review of eight trials found no study reporting adverse effects of repeated sucrose; two trials found no poorer neurological development, while one found poorer neurological development in preterm infants under 31 weeks' gestation who received more than 10 doses in 24 hours in the first week of life, compared with infants given fewer doses; no study reported long-term development. In a trial in 93 stable preterm newborns given sucrose or water for every potentially painful procedure for 7 days, short-term neurobehavioural scores at 40 weeks did not differ. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
